text:
Christopher Columbus

Frederick’s hand hovered over the vial, the liquid inside shimmering with an unnatural, pearlescent glow. The draft from the hidden chamber had died down, leaving a heavy silence that pressed against his eardrums. He looked at the runes, then at the vial, and finally at the dark entrance of the chamber where the outside world waited.

In the original timeline, Frederick chose destruction, shattering the vial and sealing the chamber forever. But in this alternative ending, he chose differently.

He uncorked the vial and drank.

The effect was not immediate. There was no surge of power, no blinding light. Instead, a profound stillness settled over him. He felt the weight of centuries lift from his shoulders, replaced by a cold, detached clarity. He looked at his hands; the age spots and wrinkles seemed to fade, not instantly, but as if time itself had stopped flowing around him.

He did not leave the chamber. Instead, he sat on the stone floor, the ancient book still open before him. He realized that eternal life was not a gift of vitality, but a curse of observation. He would watch the world change, civilizations rise and fall, and languages evolve, all while he remained unchanged.

Years turned into decades, then centuries. The hidden chamber became a legend, then a myth, then forgotten entirely. Frederick remained, a silent guardian of a secret no one else knew existed. He did not claim immortality for himself in the way he had imagined; he claimed it for the knowledge. He became the living archive, the eternal witness to the truth that some secrets are meant to be kept, not shared. And in the quiet of the endless night, Frederick smiled, for he had finally understood the true meaning of the runes: not to live forever, but to remember forever.
